content: Michael Faraday, FRS (September 22, 1791 – August 25, 1867), was an English chemist and physicist who made significant contributions to the fields of electromagnetism and electrochemistry. He investigated the magnetic field surrounding a conductor carrying a direct current and laid the groundwork for the concept of the magnetic field in physics. Faraday discovered electromagnetic induction, diamagnetism, and the principles of electrolysis. He demonstrated that magnetism could influence light rays and established a fundamental relationship between these two phenomena. Faraday's inventions of electromagnetic rotary devices were pivotal in the development of electric motor technology, and his work was instrumental in making electricity a practical resource for technological applications. As a chemist, he discovered benzene, studied chlorine clathrate hydrates, invented an early version of the Bunsen burner, and introduced the system of oxidation numbers. He also popularized terms such as anode, cathode, electrode, and ion. Despite having little formal education and limited knowledge of advanced mathematics, Faraday became one of the most influential scientists in history. Some historians regard him as the greatest experimentalist in the history of science. The SI unit of capacitance, the farad, and the Faraday constant, which represents the charge of one mole of electrons, are named in his honor. Faraday's law of induction states that a time-varying magnetic field generates a proportional electromotive force. Faraday was the first Fullerian Professor of Chemistry at the Royal Institution of Great Britain, a lifetime appointment. He was born in Newington Butts, South London, to a poor family. His father, James Faraday, was a blacksmith and a member of the Sandemanian sect of Christianity. Michael Faraday, one of four children, received only a basic education and largely taught himself. At the age of 14, he became an apprentice to a local bookbinder and bookseller, George Riebau. During his apprenticeship, he read extensively, including Isaac Watts' The Improvement of the Mind, and developed a keen interest in science, particularly electricity. He was inspired by Jane Marcet's Conversations in Chemistry. At the age of 20, Faraday attended lectures by the renowned chemist Humphry Davy and John Tatum. Faraday later sent Davy a 300-page book of notes he had taken during the lectures, which impressed Davy. When Davy injured his eyesight in a nitrogen trichloride accident, he hired Faraday as his secretary. Faraday eventually became a Chemical Assistant at the Royal Institution. Despite facing class-based prejudice and being treated poorly by Davy's wife during a European tour, Faraday gained exposure to the European scientific elite and their ideas. Faraday's early chemical work included studies of chlorine and the discovery of two new carbon chlorides. He conducted experiments on gas diffusion, liquefied several gases, and investigated steel alloys and optical glass. One of his heavy glass specimens became historically significant when he observed the rotation of the plane of polarized light in a magnetic field and discovered diamagnetism. Faraday also invented an early version of the Bunsen burner and worked extensively on the general methods of chemistry. In 1820, Faraday synthesized compounds of carbon and chlorine and determined the composition of chlorine clathrate hydrate. He discovered the laws of electrolysis and introduced terms like anode, cathode, electrode, and ion, many of which were coined by William Whewell. Faraday was the first to report the optical properties of gold colloids, which marked the beginning of nanoscience. Faraday's most significant work was in electricity and magnetism. In 1821, inspired by Hans Christian Ørsted's discovery of electromagnetism, Faraday built devices to demonstrate electromagnetic rotation, laying the foundation for modern electromagnetic technology. However, his failure to credit Davy and Wollaston for their influence led to controversy, and Faraday temporarily withdrew from electromagnetic research. After Davy's death in 1829, Faraday resumed his work and, in 1831, discovered electromagnetic induction. He demonstrated that a changing magnetic field produces an electric field, a principle later mathematically modeled as Faraday's law and incorporated into Maxwell's equations. Faraday constructed the first electric dynamo, the precursor to modern power generators. He also demonstrated that electric charge resides only on the exterior of a conductor, a principle now known as the Faraday cage. Near the end of his career, Faraday proposed that electromagnetic forces extend into empty space, a concept initially rejected but later foundational to field theory. Faraday's work on diamagnetism and the Faraday effect established a connection between magnetism and light. He showed that the plane of polarization of light could be rotated by a magnetic field. His experiments and clear communication of ideas made him an exceptional experimentalist, though his mathematical abilities were limited. James Clerk Maxwell later formalized Faraday's work into a set of equations that underpin modern electromagnetic theory. Faraday also engaged in public service, investigating coal mine explosions, air pollution, and industrial contamination. He advised on lighthouse construction, ship corrosion prevention, and the cleaning of art collections. Faraday refused to develop chemical weapons during the Crimean War on ethical grounds. He was a devout Christian and a member of the Sandemanian denomination, serving as an elder in their church. Faraday declined a knighthood and twice refused the presidency of the Royal Society. In 1848, he was granted a grace-and-favor house at Hampton Court, where he retired in 1858. Faraday died on August 25, 1867, and was buried in the Sandemanian plot at Highgate Cemetery. A memorial plaque in Westminster Abbey honors him near Isaac Newton's tomb. Faraday's legacy includes numerous honors, such as his image on British £20 banknotes and institutions named after him. His writings, including Chemical Manipulation and Experimental Researches in Electricity, remain influential. Faraday's contributions to science, particularly his experimental methods and discoveries, continue to inspire generations of scientists.
